title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarking, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document consolidates our serving runtime reference: architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling/playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes cadence, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is the canonical team wiki entry for on-call engineers, runtime developers, and performance owners.

Scope
- Hosts the runtime architecture summary and ownership.
- Kernel and scheduling configuration guidance and tuning knobs.
- Profiling playbook for latency/cost regressions.
- Benchmarking suite usage and CI integration.
- Release and rollout checklist for runtime changes.
- Common known issues and workarounds.
- Runbooks for high-latency, OOMs, and KV cache problems.

Owner and contacts
- Primary owner: eng/serving-runtime (team lead: Aisha Patel)
- On-call rotation: serving-runtime-sre (pager duty)
- Primary reviewers: Ravi Kumar, Elena García

Architecture summary

High level components
- Frontend API Gateway: HTTP(S) ingress, rate-limiting, auth; routes to runtime pools.
- Router/Smart-Router: request routing by policy (latency, cost, region, model variant).
- Serving Runtime (workers): GPU-optimized inference engine. Implements batching, KV cache, token streaming, and quantization-friendly execution.
- Model Store: artifact storage (S3-compatible) with versioning and metadata.
- Orchestration: autoscaler, placement controller, and capacity manager for Dedicated pools.
- Observability: per-route traces, token-level cost metrics, GPU telemetry, and p95/p99 tail-latency dashboards.

Service boundaries and contracts
- RPC contract between Router and Runtime: JSON framed over gRPC with headers for model id, version, routing policy, and trace id. (See api-standards page for proto).
- SLOs: 99.9% requests < 200ms p50/p95 targets depend on model family (documented in per-model profile).
- Backwards compatibility: runtime must accept older KV cache manifest schema for 12 months.

Kernel scheduling & execution model

Goals
- Maximize GPU utilization without increasing tail latency.
- Provide predictable per-request latency for latency-sensitive customers.
- Support mixed workloads (chat, streaming, embeddings) on the same pool with QoS.

Key primitives
- Continuous batching: runtime aggregates inflight requests up to dynamic batch size determined by latency budget and sequence length distribution.
- Kernel selection: at runtime the operator chooses between fast-f32 kernels, int8/4 quantized kernels, and mixed-precision kernels depending on model profile and quantization setting.
- KV cache placement: per-request KV cache shards pinned to CUDA memory pages with eviction policy LRU with priority boost for pinned sessions.
- QoS lanes: requests are tagged latency-critical or throughput-optimized; scheduler reserves slots for latency-critical lanes.

Tunable knobs (common configs)
- max_batch_bytes: maximum aggregate token budget per batch (default: "200000").
- min_batch_time_ms: how long to wait to accumulate batch (default: "2").
- lane_reservation_fraction: fraction of GPU SM blocks reserved for latency-critical lanes (default: "0.15").
- kernel_preload: enabled/disabled ("enabled" by default) — preloads frequently used kernels into GPU memory.
- kvcache_shard_size_mb: shard target size (default: "256").

Recommendations
- For p50/p95-sensitive models (chat): set min_batch_time_ms <= 2ms and lane_reservation_fraction >= 0.1.
- For cost-sensitive high-throughput workloads (embeddings): increase max_batch_bytes and min_batch_time_ms to allow larger effective batching.
- Always enable kernel_preload for production pools that serve the same model family; disable for heavy model churn during canaries.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run profiling
- Latency increase detected: p95 or p99 increase > 20% for > 5 minutes.
- Cost regression detected: per-token compute cost up > 15% vs baseline.

Quick triage checklist
1) Validate incident: check dashboards (p95, p99, GPU utilization, queue length) and traces for error spikes.
2) Identify affected model(s) and pool(s).
3) Check recent deployments: model version, runtime binary, kernel updates, quantization profile changes in last 24–72 hrs.
4) If latency spike correlates with increased batch sizes or queue length, suspect scheduling/backpressure misconfiguration.

Profiling steps
- Use trace capture (otel) for 2–10 minutes of representative traffic. Export spans with per-token timing.
- Run GPU profiler (nsys or nvprof): capture 30s window during high load. Flags: --capture-range=nvtx --sample=cpu. Collect kernels, memory copy times, SM occupancy.
- Collect runtime logs: batching debug (enable transient log level on route), kernel-selection trace, kvcache evictions.
- Local reproduce harness: run benchmark with the same seed traffic using bench-runner (see benchmarking section).

Commands (examples)
- Capture OTEL traces: curl -H "traceparent:..." https://router.internal/... (use span sampling 100% for debug).
- GPU capture (on node): sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/profile -t cuda,osrt --trace=nvtx --duration 30s --export=sqlite /usr/bin/runtime-worker --run-test
- Export runtime logs: ./rtctl dump-logs --pool mypool --since 2026-02-28T10:00:00Z --level debug > /tmp/logs.gz

Interpreting results - common signatures
- High memcpy times + low kernel occupancy: memory-bound; check model weights placement (page-locked) and kernel_preload.
- High kernel launch latency + many small kernels: kernel fusion opportunity; file an perf task.
- Growing KV cache evictions coincident with tail latency: reduce kvcache_shard_size_mb or increase shard count and tune LRU weights.

Benchmarking suite

Purpose
- Standardize perf/cost baselines across model variants, hardware types, and sequence length distributions. Benchmarks feed: model profiles, autoscaling policies, and release gating.

Repo and CI integration
- bench-runner repo: git@internal:redwood/bench-runner.git (CI job: bench/merge)
- CI job triggers: nightly full-suite and per-PR smoke tests that run short workload against a small local runtime image.

Benchmark profiles
- latency-chat: sequence length 64/256 mix, closed-loop request rate for p95/p99.
- throughput-embeddings: batch aggregation heavy, sequence length 1–4, measure tokens/sec and cost/token.
- kvcache-heavy: long conversations with repeated prefixes to measure cache hit ratio and reuse.

How to run locally
- Start local runtime image: docker-compose -f docker/bench.yml up --build -d
- Run bench: ./bench-runner --profile latency-chat --model redwood-7b --concurrency 32 --duration 60s --out /tmp/bench.json
- Compare to baseline: ./bench-compare --baseline artifacts/baselines/redwood-7b-latency.json /tmp/bench.json

Interpreting metrics
- p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, cost_per_token, gpu_utilization, kvcache_hit_rate. Bench runner produces a summarized CSV and JSON. CI fails a gating check if p95 increases > 10% vs baseline or cost/token increases > 12%.

Release notes and rollout playbook

Release cadence
- Runtime binary: bi-weekly minor releases; emergency patches as needed.
- Kernel pack: monthly, pinned per minor release.
- Quantization/Model-profiles: independent; release only after evals pass.

Pre-release checklist
1) All unit and integration tests green.
2) Benchmark smoke: perf regressions < 5% for targeted models.
3) Security scan and license checks complete.
4) Release notes drafted: list changes, risk, rollout plan, and rollback steps.

Canary rollout procedure
1) Deploy runtime change to 1–2 canary nodes in a staging pool.
2) Run bench-runner smoke profile and production traffic shadow for 30–60 minutes.
3) Check metrics: p50/p95/p99, tail-latency traces, GPU mem usage, OOMs.
4) If green, expand to 10% of capacity for 2 hours, then 50% for 6 hours, then full.
5) If regression observed at any stage: rollback to previous runtime image and notify stakeholders.

Rollback steps
- Trigger: p95 increase > 15% or any OOMs affecting >1% requests during rollout window.
- Action: use deployment manager: ./deployctl rollback --service runtime --to-tag vX.Y.Z-previous and shrink new pool by 100%.

Known issues & mitigations (operational summary)

1) Symptom: Periodic tail latency spikes aligned with kernel warmup.
   - Root cause: Kernel JIT/warmup causing first-use latency.
   - Mitigation: Enable kernel_preload and schedule warming jobs during low traffic windows.

2) Symptom: GPU OOM after large-batch requests from corner-case customer.
   - Root cause: Unbounded request with sequence length spike.
   - Mitigation: Enforce per-request sequence_length_limit and max_batch_bytes. Add admission control that caps requests by token budget.

3) Symptom: KV cache thrashing leading to increased latency.
   - Root cause: Too-small kvcache_shard_size or high churn of session ids.
   - Mitigation: Increase shard size, tune LRU weights, and support sticky session routing for long conversations.

4) Symptom: Regression after kernel pack upgrade on A100 nodes only.
   - Root cause: New kernel path uses different shared memory settings causing reduced occupancy on specific SM sizes.
   - Mitigation: Revert kernel pack for affected node pool and open perf investigation ticket. Add targeted smoke tests for A100 in CI.

Operational runbooks (playbook excerpts)

Runbook: High p95/p99 latency (on-call)
1) Acknowledge page and assign primary responder.
2) Short triage: check if issue is global or single pool. Use dashboard filters.
3) If queue length > 10k or GPU util < 30% with long queues: suspect scheduling misconfiguration.
4) If GPU util > 90% and kernel times high: open perf investigation and consider scale-out.
5) Temporary mitigations: redirect traffic to dedicated low-latency pool, increase pool size, or roll back recent runtime release.
6) Post-incident: run profiling playbook, update the incident report, and create regression alert.

Runbook: GPU OOMs
1) Identify OOM logs: node-level /var/log/nvidia*.log and runtime traces.
2) Find the offending model and request (trace id).
3) Quarantine node: mark as unschedulable and cordon.
4) Restart runtime on node with debug logging and collect heap/dump.
5) If OOM due to single request, add per-request limits and communicate to customer.
6) If OOM due to kernel change: rollback kernel pack for pool and open ticket.

Team wiki and how-tos
- Adding a new model to serving: follow model-onboarding checklist (link) — includes profiling, quantization-profile creation, and bench baseline creation.
- Updating kernel pack: coordinate with runtime team, create per-hardware smoke jobs, and update CI matrix.
- Tuning schedules: maintain per-pool tuning docs under /ops/tuning (examples for chat vs embeddings).

Appendices
A. Useful commands
- rtctl: runtime control tool (examples)
  - ./rtctl scale --pool $POOL --replicas 5
  - ./rtctl set-config --pool $POOL --key kvcache_shard_size_mb --value 512
  - ./rtctl dump-state --pool $POOL --out /tmp/state.json

B. Example config snippet (YAML)
```yaml
pool_name: chat-latency-1
replicas: 8
node_selector: gpu-type=a100
runtime_config:
  max_batch_bytes: 200000
  min_batch_time_ms: 2
  lane_reservation_fraction: 0.15
  kernel_preload: enabled
  kvcache_shard_size_mb: 256
```

C. Incident reporting template (to be attached in postmortem)
- Incident summary
- Timeline
- Root cause
- Mitigation steps taken
- Long term action items and owners

D. Performance and cost baselines (where to find)
- Baselines are stored in artifacts/baselines/ in bench-runner repo. Use bench-compare to generate comparison reports.
